page: Amazon Web Services g7.2xlarge is an accelerated computing instance built on the Nitro System hypervisor. The hardware profile is driven by an Intel x86_64 processor delivering 8 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs running at 3.9 GHz, without simultaneous multithreading. System memory is provisioned at 32.0 GB, providing an even allocation of 4.0 GB of RAM per core.

Acceleration is anchored by one NVIDIA Blackwell RTX PRO 4500 GPU equipped with 32 GB of dedicated video memory. Local ephemeral storage includes a bundled 440 GB NVMe SSD for high-throughput caching and scratch operations. Baseline network performance is configured for 40 Gbps, though no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned by default.

Because the vCPU allocation maps directly to non-hyperthreaded physical cores, the architecture avoids compute contention during heavy parallel execution. The symmetric allocation of 32 GB system memory alongside 32 GB of GPU VRAM targets visual processing pipelines. This configuration is aligned with virtual workstations, real-time 3D rendering, video encoding, spatial computing, and moderate-scale machine learning inference.
description: Amazon Web Services g7.2xlarge is an accelerated computing instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, designed for graphics-intensive and compute-accelerated workloads. The host system features an Intel x86_64 architecture CPU clocked at 3.9 GHz with 8 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs, executing one thread per core without hyperthreading. System memory totals 32.0 GB, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Graphics processing is managed by a single NVIDIA Blackwell RTX PRO 4500 GPU with 32 GB of dedicated VRAM. Storage consists of a bundled 440 GB local NVMe SSD, complemented by a 40 Gbps baseline network interface. The combination of dedicated non-hyperthreaded compute, high-bandwidth local NVMe storage, and dedicated Blackwell workstation GPU resources makes this instance suited for graphics rendering, engineering simulation, 3D visualization, and machine learning inference workloads.
